parole.significato: a kayaker; a person who paddles a kayak
parole.testo: From kajakk (“kayak”) + roer (“rower”), literally “kayak rower”. The second element roer (“rower”) is derived from ro (“to row”) + -er (“agent noun suffix”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to row”). Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk kajakkroar and Danish kajakroer.

parole.significato: kayak sport; kayaking practised as a sport
parole.testo: From kajakk (“kayak”) + sport (“sport”), literally “kayak sport”. The second element sport is borrowed from English sport, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to lead, pass over”). Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk kajakksport, Danish kajaksport and German Kajaksport.

parole.significato: a kayak trip; a trip or excursion made by kayak
parole.testo: From kajakk (“kayak”) + tur (“trip, journey”), literally “kayak trip”. The second element tur (“trip, journey”) is borrowed from French tour, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn”). Compare the parallel formations Danish kajaktur and Swedish kajaktur.

parole.significato: the left hand
parole.testo: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *geybʰ- (“bowed, curved, crooked, skew”), and cognate with Lithuanian gei̇̃bti (“to decline, become weak”), Latin gibber (“hunch, hump”).

parole.significato: an umiak; a large, open traditional Inuit boat, consisting of a wooden or bone frame traditionally covered with animal…
parole.testo: From kone (“woman, wife”) + båt (“boat”), literally “woman boat”, referring to the traditional use of the vessel, which was commonly rowed by women. The first element is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn (“woman”). Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk konebåt and Danish konebåd.

parole.significato: a racing kayak; a narrow, lightweight and relatively unstable kayak designed for speed and use in competitions
parole.testo: From racer (“racer, racing vehicle”) + kajakk (“kayak”), literally “racer kayak”. The first element racer is borrowed from English racer, from race + -er, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁s- (“to flow, rush”). Compare the parallel formation Danish racerkajak.
